scope: The structural format of a cookbook ingredient (an atomic component spec): the file's applicability, its frontmatter, the H1 title, the ordered list of 22 sections with their MAY-omit status, and what each section must hold (Overview, Behavioral Requirements, Appearance, States, Accessibility, Conformance Test Vectors, Edge Cases, Configuration, Deep Linking, Localization, Accessibility Options, Feature Flags, Analytics, Privacy, Logging, Platform Notes, Reference Implementations, Design Decisions, Compliance, Change History), the template's default content, and the component-recipe section list that template-conformance repeats. Requirement-keyword case and lint severity belong to requirement-keywords and are left out.
research_type: verification of an existing draft and its template against standards bodies, platform owners, tool and design-system documentation, plus discovery of practices the draft lacks

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: Each of the 35 rules in the brief was checked against primary sources: standards bodies (IETF/RFC Editor, W3C, OASIS), the platform owners' own documentation (Apple, Google/Android/Firebase/Play/Flutter, Microsoft), the tools' own documentation (markdownlint, Vale, JSON Schema, ReSpec, Jekyll, OpenFeature, SemVer) and design systems' own templates (PatternFly, GOV.UK, Material, Fluent). Each claim quotes the fetched source verbatim; secondary practitioner articles are used only for the expert's view, where no primary source covers the point.
methodology.search_strategy: Topic-only web searches and direct fetches of the canonical pages: document-structure and section-order guidance in specification style guides, conformance and test-assertion guidance, structured rule formats, required-heading linters and schema validators, component documentation templates, and each platform's accessibility, deep-linking, localization, logging, analytics and privacy pages.
methodology.inclusion: Primary sources from the owner of the standard, platform, tool or design system, fetched and quoted verbatim on 2026-11-21; secondary sources only where no primary covers the point, said so in the trust basis.
methodology.exclusion: Pages that could not be fetched (Segment, GitLab Pajamas, EightShapes), sources with no quotable text on the point, and anything on requirement-keyword case or lint severity (requirement-keywords' topic).
methodology.scoring: Trust is a 0-100 blend: authority 30, independent corroboration 25, accuracy 20, currency 10, transparency 15, judged at the technical-medium bar; secondary sources are capped at 72. Every research claim's verbatim words were found at one publisher, so each is 'single'; prior claims are 'uncorroborated' and score 0.

summary: Specification style guides (RFC 7322, the W3C QA framework, the ACT Rules Format) and design-system templates (PatternFly, GOV.UK) support a fixed section order with named headings, but only at recommended strength inside the body, with a short required core and the rest labelled optional; none supports a 22-section MUST order. They agree on a conformance clause, testable requirements and test vectors with expected outcomes, and the W3C outcome vocabularies include 'inapplicable', which the draft's passed/failed/partial lacks. Where a section does not apply, IETF and W3C keep it with an explicit 'none' statement in the source while publishers may hide it in the rendered form. Platform owners contradict three template defaults: one 44x44pt tap target (Apple's minimum varies by platform, Android uses 48dp, Windows 40px, WCAG AA 24px), a custom URL scheme for Apple deep links (Apple strongly recommends universal links) and dotted analytics event names (Firebase allows only letters, digits and underscores). Section structure can be machine-checked with markdownlint MD043 or a custom rule, Vale, or a JSON Schema over the parsed sections; MD043 alone cannot name an optional heading.
open_questions: Should an inapplicable section be omitted, or kept with a one-line 'not applicable' note in the source (IETF/W3C practice) and hidden only in a rendered form (GOV.UK practice)?
Should ingredients split into UI and infrastructure variants with their own section lists, or keep one schema that applies UI-only sections conditionally (JSON Schema if/then)?
Which of the formatting checks should become a schema or lint rule rather than prose: the section order, the frontmatter fields, the H1-equals-title check?
Should the template's tap-target default be one value, a per-platform table (Apple per platform, Android 48dp, Windows 40px) or the WCAG 2.2 AA 24px floor with 44px as the enhanced target?
Should analytics event names use dots, or underscores to fit Firebase's naming limits?
Should the Apple deep-linking row show a universal link instead of a custom URL scheme?
Should the compliance status vocabulary keep 'partial', or adopt EARL's passed/failed/cantTell/inapplicable/untested?
Should the section-order and section-presence rules stay MUST where the sources support only recommended strength?
Should the template keep approved-by and approved-date, which no source and no required-field list prescribes?
Should 'loading' stay among the default states, given that no platform's state list includes it?
Should the H1 duplicate the frontmatter title, given that markdownlint's default treats a front-matter title as the top-level heading?
limitations: Segment's analytics spec, GitLab's Pajamas component template and EightShapes' component-documentation articles could not be fetched (403 or load failure), so they are absent.
The W3C Security and Privacy Questionnaire gave no quotable text on a privacy section's fields.
No Android or Windows logging guidance equivalent to Apple's subsystem/category was fetched; the Logging findings are Apple-only.
No source prescribes the frontmatter field list, the approved-by/approved-date fields or a 'loading' state; those remain cookbook policy.
Apple's Human Interface Guidelines were read through their JSON endpoint, and most pages carry no date.
No claim's verbatim words were found at two independent publishers, so every research claim is 'single' even where publishers agree in substance.
Requirement-keyword case and lint severity are left to requirement-keywords and were not researched here.
The derived Reference Implementations section is cookr behaviour; no external source covers it.
The placement of Platform Notes after the core sections and of Change History at the end rests on observed page layouts (Apple HIG, Keep a Changelog) without quotable text on placement.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.
